entry.sum: Column addition and subtraction add or subtract whole numbers of any size one place at a time, from the ones leftwards, using only one-digit facts. A column that reaches ten passes one unit to the next column (carrying); a column that is short takes one unit from the next column and turns it into ten (exchanging, or borrowing). Both steps only regroup place-value units, which is why the methods are always right.
key: a - b = c \iff c + b = a
entry.why: They are the first real algorithms most people learn, and the same carry and exchange steps run inside long multiplication, decimal arithmetic, arithmetic in other bases and the adder circuits of computers.

links.note: binary adders and subtractors carry and borrow digit by digit; subtraction is done by adding a complement

blocks.body: Adding $3{,}476 + 2{,}858$ or subtracting $2{,}000 - 357$ by counting is hopeless. The column methods reduce any such sum or difference to one-digit facts such as $7 + 8 = 15$ ([[addition-subtraction]]): write the numbers one under the other, place under place, and work one column at a time from the right. When a column produces ten or more of a unit, ten of them are traded for one of the next unit; when a column is short, one of the next unit is traded for ten. Both trades only regroup place-value units, which is why the methods are always right.

blocks.title: Column addition
blocks.body:
In $47 + 38$ the ones give $7 + 8 = 15$, that is 1 ten and 5 ones. Write the 5 in the ones column and carry the ten, as a small 1, into the tens column, where $1 + 4 + 3 = 8$ tens. The sum is 85. A carry is always one unit of the next place, made from ten of this one.

In general, write a whole number $a$ by its digits $a_k \dots a_1 a_0$, where $a_0$ is the ones digit, $a_1$ the tens digit and so on, so that $a = a_k 10^k + \dots + a_1 10 + a_0$ ([[place-value]]). To compare two numbers place by place, pad the shorter one with zeros on the left: beside 352, the number 41 has digits 0, 4, 1. The numbers being added are the addends and the result is the sum.

blocks.caption: 47 + 38. Left: all the blocks together: 7 tens (4 plain rods from 47, 3 striped rods from 38) and 15 ones (7 plain, 8 striped). Ten of the ones (dashed box) make one new ten. Right: the same work in columns, with the new ten carried as a small 1 above the tens. The sum is 85.
blocks.alt: Seven rods of ten squares, four plain and three blue striped, labelled 7 tens. Fifteen single squares in three columns of five, seven plain and eight blue striped, labelled 15 ones; the first ten squares are inside a red dashed box labelled 10 ones = 1 new ten. On the right a column addition: 47 above 38 with a plus sign, a small red 1 above the 4, a line, and 85 below.

blocks.title: The column addition algorithm
blocks.body:
To add $a$ and $b$:

1. Write $b$ under $a$ with the ones digits in one column, the tens digits in the column to its left, and so on. Draw a line underneath.
2. In the ones column the carry is $c_0 = 0$.
3. In column $i$ form the column total $t_i = a_i + b_i + c_i$. Write its ones digit $s_i$ below the line and carry its tens digit $c_{i+1}$ to the next column: $t_i = s_i + 10\,c_{i+1}$.
4. Move one column left and repeat. After the last column, a carry that is not 0 is written in front. When at most ten numbers are added it is a single digit, the leading digit of the sum.

Three or more numbers are added the same way; the column total just has more terms.

blocks.solution: Ones: $6 + 7 = 13$, write 3 and carry 1 ten. Tens: $1 + 5 + 6 = 12$ tens, write 2 and carry 1 hundred. Hundreds: $1 + 4 + 1 = 6$. The sum is 623. The carry out of the tens column is a hundred: each carry is worth one unit of the place it moves into.

blocks.title: The algorithm is correct
blocks.body: The digits written by the algorithm, headed by the final carry if it is not 0, are the digits of $a + b$. With two addends every carry, the final one included, is 0 or 1.

In expanded form, $a + b = (a_0 + b_0) + (a_1 + b_1)10 + (a_2 + b_2)10^2 + \dots$: the commutative and associative laws let us collect like units, ones with ones and tens with tens. Lining up the columns is exactly what makes each column a sum of like units.

A column total can exceed 9, so this is not yet a numeral. Regroup from the right. If the ones total is $t_0 = s_0 + 10c_1$, then $t_0$ ones are $s_0$ ones and $c_1$ tens; the $c_1$ tens join the tens column, whose total becomes $t_1 = a_1 + b_1 + c_1$ tens, and so on. Each step changes nothing, because

$$t_i 10^i = s_i 10^i + c_{i+1} 10^{i+1}.$$

At the end $a + b = c_{k+1}10^{k+1} + s_k 10^k + \dots + s_0$ with every $s_i$ between 0 and 9 and, as shown next, $c_{k+1}$ equal to 0 or 1. That is a numeral, and a number has only one numeral, so it is the numeral of $a + b$.

For the carries: $c_0 = 0$, and if $c_i \le 1$ then $t_i \le 9 + 9 + 1 = 19$, so $c_{i+1} \le 1$. Column by column, every carry is 0 or 1.

blocks.solution:
Line up the ones; 861 has no thousands and no ten thousands, which is the same as digits 0 there.

1. Ones: $7 + 1 + 6 = 14$, write 4, carry 1.
2. Tens: $1 + 5 + 6 + 9 = 21$, write 1, carry 2.
3. Hundreds: $2 + 3 + 8 + 5 = 18$, write 8, carry 1.
4. Thousands: $1 + 1 + 0 + 8 = 10$, write 0, carry 1.
5. Ten thousands: $1 + 2 = 3$.

The sum is 30,814. With three addends a carry of 2 is possible, and a column total of exactly 10 still writes its 0, which holds the thousands place.

blocks.title: Line up the ones, not the left edges
blocks.body: Writing 46 under 523 with the 4 under the 5 puts the 4 in the hundreds column and the 6 in the tens: it adds 460, giving $523 + 460 = 983$. With ones under ones, $523 + 46 = 569$. Numbers of different lengths are aligned at the right.

items.q: Someone adds $69 + 57$ and writes 1116. What went wrong, and what is the sum?
items.a: The ones total $9 + 7 = 16$ was written whole instead of as 6 with 1 ten carried, and then $6 + 5 = 11$ was written in front of it. Correctly: write 6, carry 1; tens $1 + 6 + 5 = 12$. The sum is 126.

items.hint: Three of the four columns carry.
items.solution: Ones $6 + 8 = 14$: write 4, carry 1. Tens $1 + 7 + 5 = 13$: write 3, carry 1. Hundreds $1 + 4 + 8 = 13$: write 3, carry 1. Thousands $1 + 3 + 2 = 6$. The sum is 6,334.

items.hint: Start at the ones: $7 + y$ must end in 5. Keep track of the carry.
items.solution: Ones: $7 + y$ ends in 5 and is at most 16, so $7 + y = 15$, $y = 8$, carry 1. Tens: $x + 8 + 1$ ends in 6 and lies between 9 and 18, so it is 16, $x = 7$, carry 1. Hundreds: $1 + 4 + 3 = 8$, as required. So $477 + 388 = 865$.

items.q: Prove that when $m$ numbers are added in columns, every carry is at most $m - 1$. Is this bound reached for $m = 3$?
items.hint: Imitate the proof for two addends: suppose the carry in is at most $m - 1$ and bound the column total.
items.solution: The first carry is 0. If the carry into a column is at most $m - 1$, the column total is at most $9m + (m - 1) = 10m - 1$, so its tens digit, the next carry, is at most $m - 1$. Hence every carry is at most $m - 1$. For $m = 3$ the bound 2 is reached: $9 + 9 + 9 = 27$ carries 2. In particular, with at most ten addends every carry is at most 9, a single digit.

items.q: Show that when 1 is added to a number $n$, the number of carries equals the number of 9s at the right-hand end of $n$. How many carries does $99{,}999 + 1$ make?
items.hint: A column carries exactly when its total is 10.
items.solution: Adding 1 means adding 1 in the ones column and 0 elsewhere. A column with carry-in 1 (or the ones column, which receives the 1) totals its digit plus 1; that is 10, and carries 1, exactly when the digit is 9. So the carries run leftwards through the trailing 9s, turning each into 0, and stop at the first digit that is not 9, which goes up by 1. For $99{,}999 + 1 = 100{,}000$ there are five carries, one per nine.

blocks.title: Column subtraction
blocks.body: For $a - b$ with $a \ge b$ the minuend $a$ is written on top and the subtrahend $b$ below, place under place; the result is the difference. Since $a \ge b$, the number $b$ has no more digits than $a$, and it is padded with zeros on the left. Each column is top digit minus bottom digit, never the other way round.

blocks.title: The column subtraction algorithm
blocks.body:
To find $a - b$ with $a \ge b$:

1. Write $b$ under $a$ with the places lined up.
2. Work from the ones column leftwards. If the top digit (as it now stands) is at least the bottom digit, write their difference below the line.
3. If it is smaller, exchange: reduce the top digit of the next column to the left by 1 and add 10 to this top digit; then subtract.
4. If the digit to the left is 0, it has nothing to give. Exchange into it first from further left, so it becomes 10; then it gives 1 and ends as 9.

Leading zeros of the result are dropped: $500 - 500$ gives 000, that is 0.

blocks.title: Exchanging is correct
blocks.body: An exchange never changes the value of the top number. When every column has been dealt with, the digits written are the digits of $a - b$, and because $a \ge b$ the leftmost column never needs a unit from beyond the number.

An exchange rewrites $a$ using $10^{i+1} = 10 \times 10^i$: one unit of place $i + 1$ becomes ten units of place $i$. For instance

$$52 = 5 \times 10 + 2 = 4 \times 10 + 12,$$

and then $(40 + 12) - (20 + 7) = (40 - 20) + (12 - 7) = 25$.

In general, write $b = b_k 10^k + \dots + b_0$, with zeros in front if $b$ is shorter. After the exchanges $a = a'_k 10^k + \dots + a'_0$, where each $a'_i$ is at least $b_i$; some $a'_i$ may be as large as 18, so this is not a numeral, but its value is still $a$. Subtracting like units,

$$a - b = (a'_k - b_k)10^k + \dots + (a'_0 - b_0).$$

Each $a'_i - b_i$ is a digit from 0 to 9:

- If column $i$ was not short, $a'_i$ is a digit (perhaps lowered by 1) that is at least $b_i$, so $a'_i - b_i$ lies between 0 and 9.
- If column $i$ was short, its digit $d$ was less than $b_i$ and was raised to $d + 10$; then $d + 10 - b_i$ is at least 1 and, because $d < b_i$, at most 9.
- A 0 that is raised to 10 only to pass 1 to the right ends as 9, and $9 - b_i$ is a digit.

So the right side is a numeral. A number has only one numeral, so it is the numeral of $a - b$.

The leftmost column is never short. Suppose it were, and treat $a$ as having a 0 at place $k + 1$. The exchange would leave $a'_{k+1} = -1$ there, so $a = -10^{k+1} + a'_k 10^k + \dots + a'_0$, and the written digits would be the numeral of $a - b + 10^{k+1}$. A numeral with $k + 1$ digits is less than $10^{k+1}$, so $a - b < 0$, which contradicts $a \ge b$.

blocks.solution:
1. Ones: $2 < 9$, so exchange a ten: the 6 tens become 5 and the ones become 12. $12 - 9 = 3$.
2. Tens: $5 < 7$, exchange a hundred: the 1 hundred becomes 0 and the tens become 15. $15 - 7 = 8$.
3. Hundreds: $0 < 4$, exchange a thousand: the 2 thousands become 1 and the hundreds become 10. $10 - 4 = 6$.
4. Thousands: $1 - 0 = 1$.

The difference is 1,683. The top number was rewritten as 1 thousand, 10 hundreds, 15 tens and 12 ones, still $1{,}000 + 1{,}000 + 150 + 12 = 2{,}162$.

Step 2: one of those tens is exchanged for ten ones, so the 10 tens become 9 and the 4 ones become 14. Then 14 - 8 = 6, 9 - 2 = 7 and 2 - 1 = 1: the difference is 176.
blocks.alt: Two column subtractions of 304 minus 128. Step 1: the 3 and the 0 are struck through in red, with a small red 2 and 10 above them; label 1 hundred = 10 tens. Step 2: as step 1, but the 10 is also struck through in blue with a 9 above it, and the 4 is struck through in blue with 14 above it; the answer line shows 176; label 1 ten = 10 ones.

blocks.body: Subtract $304 - 128$, where the tens digit of the top number is 0.
blocks.solution:
The ones need a ten, but 304 has no tens. Exchange a hundred first: 2 hundreds, 10 tens, 4 ones. Now exchange one of those tens: 2 hundreds, 9 tens, 14 ones, and indeed $200 + 90 + 14 = 304$. Then $14 - 8 = 6$, $9 - 2 = 7$, $2 - 1 = 1$, and the difference is 176.

The 0 ends as 9 because it first receives ten and then gives one away. With several zeros the chain is longer: $2{,}000 = 1{,}000 + 900 + 90 + 10$. Such chains can be avoided. An exchange happens only where a top digit is less than the bottom one, so $999 - n$ never exchanges, as every top digit is 9; and $1{,}000 - n = (999 - n) + 1$.

blocks.title: Two classic bugs
blocks.body: A common error is to take the smaller digit from the larger in every column, whichever is on top: $74 - 38$ becomes $8 - 4 = 4$ and $7 - 3 = 4$, giving 44 instead of 36. Another is to add the 10 but forget to reduce the digit to the left: $14 - 8 = 6$ and $7 - 3 = 4$, so 46. The second breaks the invariant of the proof, that the rewritten top number is still the top number: with the 7 left unreduced it is $70 + 14 = 84$, not 74. Adding back catches both: $44 + 38 = 82$ and $46 + 38 = 84$.

blocks.title: Zeros in the top number
blocks.body: A common error is to treat $0 - 6$ as 6: in $207 - 64$ the tens give 6 and the answer becomes 263 instead of 143. Another comes when exchanging through a zero, as in $504 - 108$: the 0 is changed to 9 and the ones to 14, but the 5 hundreds are left alone. Then $14 - 8 = 6$, $9 - 0 = 9$, $5 - 1 = 4$, giving 496. The invariant exposes it: the top number has silently become $500 + 90 + 14 = 604$. Correctly, 504 is 4 hundreds, 9 tens and 14 ones, and $504 - 108 = 396$.

blocks.title: Other ways to subtract
blocks.body: Each finds $425 - 278 = 147$; they differ in which fact about subtraction they use.

items.label: Exchange first
items.body: Make all the exchanges before any subtracting: $425 = 300 + 110 + 15$. This is the rewritten top number of the proof, with every part at least the bottom digit, written out. It buys two things: no exchange can interrupt a column, so each column is a plain subtraction, $15 - 8 = 7$, $110 - 70 = 40$, $300 - 200 = 100$; and the rewriting can be checked against 425 before any subtracting is done.

items.label: Counting up
items.body: A difference is a missing addend: $278 + ? = 425$. On a number line (figure), jump from 278 to the next ten, 280 (2), then to the next hundred, 300 (20), then to 425 (125); the jumps total $2 + 20 + 125 = 147$. Nothing is exchanged: only additions up to round numbers are used.

items.label: Same change
items.body: Adding the same number to both terms does not change a difference: $425 - 278 = 427 - 280 = 447 - 300 = 147$, and the last subtraction needs no exchange.

items.a: 503 becomes 4 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones. $13 - 7 = 6$, $9 - 4 = 5$, $4 - 2 = 2$: 256. The 0 became 10 and then 9.

items.q: Subtract $7{,}005 - 6{,}998$ in columns, then check by counting up. Why do three digits of the column answer come out as 0, and what is written?
items.hint: The ones need a ten, and the nearest unit to exchange is a thousand.
items.solution: Ones: $5 < 8$, and the tens and hundreds are 0, so exchange a thousand down the chain: 6 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 15 ones (indeed $6{,}000 + 900 + 90 + 15 = 7{,}005$). Then $15 - 8 = 7$, $9 - 9 = 0$, $9 - 9 = 0$, $6 - 6 = 0$. The columns give 0007; the three zeros come from equal digits, and they are leading zeros, so they are dropped and the answer is 7. Counting up: 6,998 to 7,000 is 2, and 7,000 to 7,005 is 5, so $2 + 5 = 7$.

items.q: Someone writes $602 - 357 = 355$. Which bug produces this, and what is the right answer?
items.hint: Do each column the wrong way: smaller from larger.
items.solution: Smaller from larger: $7 - 2 = 5$, $5 - 0 = 5$, $6 - 3 = 3$ gives 355. Correctly, 602 is 5 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones: $12 - 7 = 5$, $9 - 5 = 4$, $5 - 3 = 2$, so 245. Check: $245 + 357 = 602$.

items.q: Explain why $999 - n$ never needs an exchange when $n \le 999$, and use $1{,}000 - n = (999 - n) + 1$ to find $1{,}000 - 456$.
items.hint: Every top digit is 9, the largest digit.
items.solution: Each bottom digit is at most 9, so no column is short; each digit of $999 - n$ is just 9 minus the digit of $n$. Thus $999 - 456 = 543$, and $1{,}000 - 456 = 543 + 1 = 544$. This replaces three chained exchanges by one easy addition.

items.q: Prove that $a - b = (a + k) - (b + k)$ for whole numbers with $a \ge b$, and use it to compute $6{,}000 - 2{,}987$ without any exchange.
items.hint: Let $c = a - b$, so $c + b = a$. Add $k$ to both sides.

blocks.title: Checking and choosing a method
blocks.body:
A slip in one column gives a wrong answer that looks as plausible as the right one, so answers are checked, by undoing the operation or by comparing with an estimate.

Since $a - b = c$ means exactly $c + b = a$ ([[addition-subtraction]]), a subtraction is checked by adding the difference to the bottom number, and an addition $a + b = c$ by checking $c - b = a$. The check uses the other algorithm, with carries in place of exchanges, so it does not simply repeat a slip.

blocks.solution: Add back: $2{,}286 + 1{,}797$. Ones $6 + 7 = 13$, write 3, carry 1. Tens $1 + 8 + 9 = 18$, write 8, carry 1. Hundreds $1 + 2 + 7 = 10$, write 0, carry 1. Thousands $1 + 2 + 1 = 4$. That is 4,083, so the subtraction is right.

blocks.title: What an estimate can catch
blocks.body: In an addition, a carry lost on its way into column $i$ makes the answer exactly $10^i$ too small: 10 for the tens, 100 for the hundreds. Rounding both numbers to the nearest hundred gives an estimate within 100 of the true answer (to the nearest ten, within 10). So such an estimate always exposes a lost carry into the thousands or beyond, but a lost carry into the tens or hundreds can slip through.

Every step of the algorithm except the slip keeps the value, by $t_i 10^i = s_i 10^i + c_{i+1} 10^{i+1}$; the slip throws away one unit of $10^i$.

If $a = A + e$ and $b = B + f$ with $|e| \le 50$ and $|f| \le 50$, then $(a \pm b) - (A \pm B) = e \pm f$, at most 100 in size. An answer 1,000 or more from the true one is then at least 900 from the estimate. But in $101 + 199 = 300$, losing the carry into the hundreds gives 200, which is within 100 of the estimate $100 + 200 = 300$.

blocks.title: Columns are not always the best method
blocks.body: The algorithm always works, but for numbers that are close together or near a round number a mental method is shorter and safer. $402 - 398$ needs an exchange through a zero in columns, yet counting up from 398 gives $2 + 2 = 4$ at once; $164 + 36$ is $100 + 100 = 200$ because 64 and 36 make 100.

items.solution: Ones $7 + 8 = 15$: write 5, carry 1. Tens $1 + 7 + 6 = 14$: write 4, carry 1. Hundreds $1 + 3 + 3 = 7$. That is 745, so the subtraction is right.

items.q: Someone claims $583 + 249 = 722$. Use an estimate to the nearest ten to prove this wrong, then find the sum.
items.hint: The rounded sum is within 10 of the true one.
items.solution: $580 + 250 = 830$, so the true sum lies between 820 and 840; 722 is impossible. In columns: ones $3 + 9 = 12$, write 2, carry 1; tens $1 + 8 + 4 = 13$, write 3, carry 1; hundreds $1 + 5 + 2 = 8$. The sum is 832. The claim dropped both carries.

items.q: A tank holds 2,340 litres. 1,265 litres are drawn off and then 870 litres are added. How much is in it now? Would adding the 870 litres first give the same answer, and why?
items.hint: For the second part, add 1,265 to each possible answer.
items.solution:
$2{,}340 - 1{,}265$: ones $0 < 5$, exchange: 3 tens, 10 ones, $10 - 5 = 5$; tens $3 < 6$, exchange: 2 hundreds, 13 tens, $13 - 6 = 7$; hundreds $2 - 2 = 0$; thousands $2 - 1 = 1$. That is 1,075. Then $1{,}075 + 870$: ones 5; tens $7 + 7 = 14$, write 4, carry 1; hundreds $1 + 0 + 8 = 9$; thousands 1. That is 1,945 litres.

Adding first gives $3{,}210 - 1{,}265 = 1{,}945$, the same. In general $(a - b) + c = (a + c) - b$ when $a \ge b$: adding $b$ to the left side gives $(a - b) + b + c = a + c$, so the left side is the number which, added to $b$, gives $a + c$, and that is what the right side means.

items.q: The wrong answer $456 + 376 = 842$ passes an estimate to the nearest hundred. Explain why, and show that the inverse check catches it.
items.hint: How far is 842 from the true sum, and how far is the estimate allowed to be?
items.solution: The estimate $500 + 400 = 900$ allows anything from 800 to 1,000, and 842 is in that range: the error of 10 is smaller than the estimate's tolerance of 100. Adding back fails: $842 - 376 = 466$, not 456. An estimate catches large errors only; the inverse check catches any error, provided the check itself is done correctly.

rows.text: Carry, regroup and compose a ten (or a hundred) name the same step. Borrow, exchange and decompose name the reverse step, and column subtraction done this way is called the decomposition method.

Carries go above the next column or just below the addends; in subtraction the changed digits are crossed out and the new ones written above; digits of large numbers are grouped in threes with commas, as in 21,357.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
Long multiplication (separate page: Long multiplication) forms rows of partial products and adds them with this algorithm. Adding and subtracting decimals (separate page: Decimal operations) lines up the decimal points, so that tenths fall under tenths, and the carries pass across the point unchanged.

The proofs used nothing about ten except $10^{i+1} = 10 \times 10^i$. In base $b$ a column carries when it reaches $b$: in base two $1 + 1 = 10$, and $1011 + 110 = 10001$ is $11 + 6 = 17$ ([[digits-bases]]). Computer adders are this algorithm in base two, and they subtract with the same trick as $1{,}000 - n = (999 - n) + 1$: in base two, $11\dots1 - n$ needs no exchange and just swaps each digit of $n$ between 0 and 1, as in $111 - 101 = 010$.

Carries can cascade, as in $99{,}999 + 1$, but each column is visited once, so the work grows in proportion to the number of digits; counting steps like this is the study of [[algorithms]].

The ones digit of a sum or difference depends only on the ones digits of the numbers: this is arithmetic modulo 10, the beginning of [[congruences]]. And if exchanges are allowed to run on forever to the left, $0 - 1$ comes out as $\dots 9999$, a number that gives 0 when 1 is added. Taken seriously, such infinite numerals lead to the [[p-adic-numbers]].

- Line up the places; work one column at a time from the ones.
- Addition: a column total $t_i$ is written as its ones digit, and its tens digit is carried; $t_i 10^i = s_i 10^i + c_{i+1} 10^{i+1}$ keeps the value. With two addends a carry is 0 or 1.
- Subtraction: always top minus bottom; a short column takes one unit from the left as ten. An exchange never changes the top number, and a 0 exchanged through ends as 9.
- The method is correct because like units are combined and every trade uses $10^{i+1} = 10 \times 10^i$; the result is a numeral, and numerals are unique.
- Check by the inverse operation. A lost carry changes a sum by a power of ten; an estimate to the nearest hundred is within 100, so it misses small slips that the inverse check catches. Use a mental method when the numbers invite one.

checks.python:
def col_add(*nums):
    width = max(len(str(n)) for n in nums)
    c = 0; digits = []; carries = []
    for p in range(width + 2):
        t = sum((n // 10**p) % 10 for n in nums) + c
        digits.append(t % 10); c = t // 10; carries.append(c)
    return sum(d * 10**p for p, d in enumerate(digits)), carries
def col_sub(a, b):
    da = [int(x) for x in str(a)[::-1]] + [0]; db = [int(x) for x in str(b)[::-1]] + [0] * 12
    ex = []; top = None
    for p in range(len(da) - 1):
        if da[p] < db[p]:
            ex.append(p); q = p + 1
            while da[q] == 0: da[q] = 9; q += 1
            da[q] -= 1; da[p] += 10
        da[p] -= db[p]
    return sum(d * 10**p for p, d in enumerate(da)), ex

def dont_decrement_zero(a, b):
    da = [int(x) for x in str(a)[::-1]]; db = [int(x) for x in str(b)[::-1]] + [0] * 10
    for p in range(len(da)):
        if da[p] < db[p]:
            q = p + 1
            if da[q] == 0: da[q] = 9  # 0 becomes 9, the digit beyond it is left alone
            else: da[q] -= 1
            da[p] += 10
        da[p] -= db[p]
    return sum(x * 10**p for p, x in enumerate(da))

    # column addition with the carry into column i lost
    c = 0; out = 0
    for p in range(max(len(str(a)), len(str(b))) + 2):

        t = (a // 10**p) % 10 + (b // 10**p) % 10 + c
        out += (t % 10) * 10**p; c = t // 10
    return out
